findings.title: Hidden PowerShell stager (control.exe parent) opened lsass.exe with full access and read its memory on scranton.dmevals.local
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T02:58:44Z, user DMEVALS\pbeesly spawned a hidden, execution-policy-bypassing PowerShell (PID 2976) from the parent 'C:\Windows\System32\control.exe"  /name Microsoft.BackupAndRestoreCenter' — a classic APT29 stager pattern. The command line decodes a bitmap (C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\monkey.png) into shellcode and IEXes it. At 03:05:16Z that same PID 2976 opened lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) with an UNKNOWN call trace, and Security 4656/4663 confirm the handle request and a 0x10 (VM_READ) read of \Device\HarddiskVolume2\Windows\System32\lsass.exe by powershell.exe as pbeesly. This is LSASS memory credential dumping. The same actor then used WinRM to nashua.dmevals.local (wsmprovhost.exe PID 7720, also as pbeesly) which opened lsass with 0x1f3fff at 03:09:29Z. Benign lsass accessors in the same window (svchost.exe 0x1000/0x1400, AntimalwareConfig.exe, WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe, MsMpEng.exe, CollectGuestLogs.exe) are baseline AV/telemetry behaviour and are not part of this finding.

findings.title: Credential-access tooling staged: SysinternalsSuite downloaded and extracted by the same hidden PowerShell on scranton
findings.summary: The hidden PowerShell PID 2976 on scranton.dmevals.local wrote C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\SysinternalsSuite.zip at 2020-05-02T02:59:42Z, and a second PowerShell (PID 3876) extracted the suite (hostui.txt, psversion.txt, readme.txt, Eula.txt) at 03:00:27–03:00:32Z. SysinternalsSuite contains procdump, a common LSASS dumping utility, and the extraction immediately precedes the lsass access at 03:05:16Z. No procdump command line was observed in 4688/Sysmon event 1, so the actual dump utility invocation is not directly captured; the staging is nonetheless part of the same intrusion chain.

findings.title: SAM hive value write by lsass.exe on scranton is normal OS behaviour, not hive theft
findings.summary: The only SAM-related registry write in the window is HKLM\SAM\SAM\Domains\Account\F at 2020-05-02T03:19:10Z on scranton.dmevals.local, written by C:\windows\system32\lsass.exe itself (the legitimate owner of the SAM hive). No reg save/reg export, esentutl, vssadmin or hive-file copy was observed (C017/C018/C020/C021/C022 all zero hits), and the three 'SAM/SECURITY' file-create hits were only Prefetch .pf files. The 16962 event about remote SAM access restriction is a default security-descriptor notice. No evidence of SAM dumping.

findings.title: No NTDS.dit access, shadow copy or ntdsutil activity observed
findings.summary: All NTDS checks (C024–C030) returned zero hits: no ntdsutil/vssadmin/diskshadow command lines, no .dit file creation or access, no 4663 object access on ntds. The hosts in scope are member workstations/servers, not domain controllers, so NTDS extraction was not attempted in this window.

findings.title: No LSA Secrets extraction; lsass accessors are baseline AV/telemetry
findings.summary: The 326 lsass process-access events are dominated by svchost.exe (289, masks 0x1000/0x1400/0x101001/0x3000 with lsm.dll/sysmain.dll call traces), AntimalwareConfig.exe (15) and WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe (13) — normal security/telemetry behaviour. No lsadump, reg save of SECURITY\Policy\Secrets, or SECURITY hive file copy was found (C032/C035/C037/C038 zero hits). The only SECURITY-related registry writes are HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 by lsass.exe (see T1003.005). The malicious lsass access is reported under T1003.001.

findings.title: HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 writes are lsass.exe updating the cached-credential store, not extraction
findings.summary: Five writes to HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 (four on nashua.dmevals.local 03:11:40–03:15:03Z, one on scranton.dmevals.local 03:20:46Z) were all performed by C:\windows\system32\lsass.exe, the legitimate owner of the cached domain credential store, consistent with normal logon/cache refresh. No mscache/dcc2/cache-dumping command line or script was found (C040/C042/C044/C045 produced no malicious hits). Note: the actor's lsass memory read on the same hosts could have captured cached credentials in memory, but that is covered by T1003.001.

findings.title: Single 4662 replication-GUID read by machine account NEWYORK$ is not DCSync
findings.summary: One 4662 event on newyork.dmevals.local at 2020-05-01T23:16:15-04:00 shows SubjectUserName NEWYORK$ (the computer account itself) with AccessMask 0x100 on object %{11487126-e2dc-4f51-acb1-1b0df0573bb5} and property {1131f6aa-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2}. A DCSync would show a user account (not the machine account) requesting DS-Replication-Get-Changes/Get-Changes-All against the domain NC, typically repeatedly. No DCSync/Invoke-Mimikatz/lsadump script blocks were found (C049 zero hits).

findings.title: Azure Network Watcher agent ran netsh packet capture on scranton (legitimate platform telemetry)
findings.summary: On 2020-05-02 at 03:19:17Z on scranton.dmevals.local, netsh.exe was launched as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM with 'trace start capture=yes traceFile="C:\windows\TEMP\E7116ECA-DFE6-43C7-8FA8-8D3AC5AA8726\B91E06C5-1C7C-4830-9A76-74FA211560A7.etl"' and stopped 7 seconds later with 'netsh trace stop'. The parent process is the Microsoft Azure NetworkWatcherAgent.exe (/service) from C:\Packages\Plugins\Microsoft.Azure.NetworkWatcher.NetworkWatcherAgentWindows\1.4.1421.1\NetworkWatcherAgent\, and the netsh binary carries a Microsoft signature hash (SHA256=90F0822D26680C8FFD703A080C876F87695580747A3704C169E39E1A8802EA38). The same agent was also seen installing/starting itself via cmd.exe. This is the Azure Network Watcher packet-capture feature, not adversary sniffing: no pktmon/windump/tcpdump/rawcap command lines, no pcap/npcap/wpcap driver loads, no capture-related PowerShell script blocks, and no .pcap/.cap files were written anywhere in the window.

findings.title: No adversary network-sniffing tooling observed; python.exe on nashua is C2 traffic, not sniffing
findings.summary: Hunting for T1040 across all four datasets found no attacker sniffing. The suspicious activity in the window is instead lateral movement: from scranton.dmevals.local, powershell.exe launched PsExec64.exe with the plaintext credential '-u dmevals\pbeesly -p Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by -i 2 C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe' against \\NASHUA, which installed PSEXESVC and started C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe as pbeesly on nashua.dmevals.local. That python.exe then made 348 outbound TCP connections to 192.168.0.4:8443 (e.g. source 10.0.1.6:60048), i.e. command-and-control/exfiltration rather than passive capture. No pcap/npcap/wpcap image loads, no pktmon/windump/tcpdump/rawcap command lines, no capture-related PowerShell script blocks, and no .pcap/.cap files were found. The logman.exe executions on scranton are the Azure WaAppAgent stopping its own GAEvents/RTEvents collectors.

findings.title: Hidden PowerShell stager on scranton decodes a PNG-embedded payload and opens a full-access handle to lsass.exe
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user DMEVALS\pbeesly launched a screen-saver binary C:\ProgramData\victim\â€®cod.3aka3.scr (parent explorer.exe, /S) at 02:55:56Z. This is attacker input/credential capture tooling, not normal system behaviour.

findings.title: Clipboard/keystroke capture: Get-Clipboard executed in the pbeesly session on scranton after the stager ran
findings.summary: At 03:06:42Z on scranton.dmevals.local, PowerShell (PID 3852, user pbeesly, SID S-1-5-21-1830255721-3727074217-2423397540-1107) executed the script block 'Get-Clipboard' — harvesting whatever the user had copied (passwords, tokens). This follows the .scr execution (02:55:56Z) and the hidden IEX stager (02:58:44Z) on the same host/session. No SetWindowsHookEx/GetAsyncKeyState keylogger code was found in script-block logging (C065 zero hits), so the observed input capture is clipboard-based rather than a kernel/user hook keylogger.

findings.title: No fake credential-prompt / GUI input capture observed; LogonUI and consent.exe are legitimate
findings.summary: Process-creation stacking (C066) and targeted review of LogonUI.exe, consent.exe and rundll32.exe showed only expected Windows behaviour: LogonUI.exe spawned by winlogon.exe with /flags:0x4 and /flags:0x2 on scranton (03:18:30Z, 03:19:10Z), consent.exe spawned by svchost.exe for UAC on scranton and nashua, and rundll32.exe davclnt.dll,DavSetCookie for WebDAV to 192.168.0.4. No credential-prompt lookalike binaries or Get-Credential/CredentialPrompt script blocks were found (C067 zero hits).

findings.title: No web portal capture observed in the Windows telemetry
findings.summary: No evidence of web-portal credential capture (no injected browser modules, no fake login pages, no proxy/portal-hooking artefacts) was found in the Windows datasets reviewed. The only web-related activity seen was rundll32 davclnt.dll,DavSetCookie against http://192.168.0.4/webdav on scranton, which is normal WebDAV cookie handling. Zeek data does not overlap this window, so network-side portal capture cannot be assessed.

findings.title: Credential API access to lsass.exe from PowerShell and wsmprovhost with full-access masks
findings.summary: Two non-standard processes obtained full-access handles to lsass.exe: PowerShell.exe PID 2976 on scranton.dmevals.local at 03:05:16Z (0x1F3FFF and 0x1FFFFF, call trace ending in UNKNOWN module) — the same process that ran the hidden PNG-decoding IEX stager — and wsmprovhost.exe PID 7720 on nashua.dmevals.local at 03:09:29Z (0x1F3FFF, call trace through System.ni.dll / Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.Management.ni.dll, i.e. PowerShell remoting). The remaining high masks (csrss/wininit 0x1FFFFF, svchost 0x101001/0x3000) are normal system accessors. No MiniDump/comsvcs script blocks or lsass strings were found in PowerShell or other logs (C081/C082 zero hits), so the hooking is via direct process-handle access rather than a dump utility.

findings.title: No brute-force activity observed; only a single successful credential validation (4776) and no 4625 failures
findings.summary: Across windows.security (2020-05-02T02:55:25Z..03:28:09Z) there are zero 4625 failed-logon events and zero 4771 Kerberos pre-auth failures. The only authentication-failure-family event retrieved was a single 4776 credential validation on newyork.dmevals.local for user pbeesly with Status 0x0 (success), i.e. a normal successful NTLM credential check, not a guessing attempt. The 4648 explicit-credential logons on scranton/nashua are pbeesly re-using its own credentials (including via C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe on nashua) plus machine-account DWM/UMFD logons, consistent with PsExec administration rather than password guessing. The 'net' command-line hits were all svchost.exe -k netsvcs service hosts and netsh.exe trace commands, i.e. benign system processes. No evidence of brute force, guessing, spraying or stuffing in this window.

findings.title: No password-guessing pattern: zero 4625 events, no net.exe/user-enumeration guessing command lines
findings.summary: Queries for 4625 in windows.security returned zero hits, and the windows.other 'failed' message hits were unrelated (a crash-dump initialization message and a DNS PTR registration failure on scranton). Stacking sysmon process-creation command lines containing 'net' produced only svchost.exe -k netsvcs service instances and two netsh.exe trace commands — no net use / net user / password-bearing command lines. The only PowerShell script block containing a hard-coded password was the Invoke-Exfil function on scranton (user pbeesly), which uses a single static credential ('cozy' / 'MyCozyPassw0rd!') to map a WebDAV drive for exfiltration, not repeated guessing against accounts.

findings.title: No smartcard, certificate-provider or MFA-interception artefacts; explicit-credential logons are PsExec administration
findings.summary: The MFA-interception-specific indicators were benign or absent. The only registry writes touching Crypto/SCard paths were six default Windows values (Cryptography\Calais SymbolicLinkValue, CertificateTemplateCache timestamps, an SCardSvr.dll MuiCache entry) with no smartcard/MFA configuration change, and windows.other contained no SmartCard/SCardSvr/Certificate messages at all. The single PowerShell script block matching *token* was a token-attribute enumeration helper (Get-AttributesMask), not an MFA/token-theft tool. The 15 event-4648 explicit-credential logons are dominated by pbeesly (9) and are explained by PsExec64.exe -u dmevals\pbeesly against \\NASHUA (PSEXESVC.exe on nashua, TargetServerName NASHUA/localhost), plus routine DWM-1/DWM-2/UMFD-0/UMFD-1/UMFD-2 and SCRANTON$ machine-account logons from winlogon/wininit/taskhostw. Logon types were 3 (218), 5 (61), 2 (15), 10 (2), 0 (1) with no smartcard (type 8) or explicit MFA-related pattern. Zeek kerberos showed 18 success / 7 failure, and the zeek window (2020-04-30) does not overlap the Windows window, so no MFA interception can be tied to it.

On 2020-04-30 between 00:32:18 and 00:32:21 UTC, host 10.0.1.4 (scranton) used the Windows WebDAV client (user agents 'DavClnt' and 'Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir/10.0.18362') against the WebDAV server at 192.168.0.4:80, issuing OPTIONS, PROPFIND, PUT, LOCK, HEAD, PROPPATCH and UNLOCK on /webdav/OfficeSupplies.7z. The 401 responses are the client being challenged by the server and then authenticating to it; the direction of authentication is client->server, the opposite of T1187 forced authentication (where an attacker lures a victim into authenticating to an attacker-controlled listener). The archive name OfficeSupplies.7z matches the Invoke-Exfil PowerShell function seen on scranton.dmevals.local (Compress-7Zip -ArchiveFileName "$env:APPDATA\OfficeSupplies.7z"), so this traffic is best explained as exfiltration over WebDAV rather than credential coercion. No T1187 lure artifacts were found: the only shortcut file created was C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\StartUp\hostui.lnk by powershell.exe on scranton (persistence-style, not a UNC/WebDAV lure), and no WebClient/NetworkProvider registry modifications were observed.
